title: The EU Just Sanctioned Iran Over Hormuz. Hours Later, the Houthis Declared a Total Ban on Israeli Shipping in the Red Sea.
excerpt: Europe's first-ever freedom-of-navigation sanctions and Yemen's renewed shipping threat are closing two of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints simultaneously. India, which depends on both, has no good options.
body:
On Monday morning, two developments — separated by a few hours and thousands of kilometres — combined to present India with its most acute maritime trade crisis in decades.

First, the European Union approved sanctions against Iranian individuals and entities involved in disrupting transit through the Strait of Hormuz. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas confirmed the measures after a meeting with defence ministers, calling them the first-ever application of the bloc's new freedom-of-navigation sanctions framework. "Ministers were clear today that Iran's actions are unacceptable," she said.

Then, Yemen's Houthi rebels declared a "complete and total ban on Israeli maritime navigation in the Red Sea" — their first such pronouncement since the April ceasefire, and a direct threat to resume the kind of commercial shipping disruption that roiled global supply chains throughout 2024.

Together, these actions threaten the two maritime corridors that India's economy depends on most.

## Why Both Chokepoints Matter to India

The Strait of Hormuz, barely 33 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, carried roughly one-fifth of the world's oil and gas before Iran began asserting control over transit. India sourced more than 40 percent of its crude imports and 90 percent of its LPG through this corridor. Even after months of diversification, the strait remains irreplaceable for the volume of energy India consumes.

The Red Sea–Suez Canal route, meanwhile, is the primary corridor for India's non-oil trade with Europe, the Mediterranean, and the eastern seaboard of the Americas. When the Houthis last disrupted Red Sea shipping in late 2023 and 2024, container freight rates spiked by as much as 300 percent, and Indian exporters — particularly in textiles, pharmaceuticals, and auto components — saw delivery timelines blow out by weeks.

A simultaneous squeeze on both routes has no modern precedent.

## The Escalation That Triggered Both

The chain of events began on Saturday, June 7. Hezbollah fired rockets at northern Israel. Israel responded by striking Beirut's southern suburbs — the Dahieh district long associated with Hezbollah. Iran, which had warned that any Israeli attack on Beirut would trigger a direct response, launched 11 ballistic missiles at northern Israel. All were intercepted, according to the Israeli military.

Israel struck back within hours, hitting a petrochemical complex in Mahshahr, in Iran's Khuzestan province. Iran then fired a second barrage, this time targeting central and southern Israel, including the area near Dimona — home to Israel's main nuclear research facility.

By Monday morning, Iran's joint military command announced it was halting offensive operations — but warned that any further Israeli "aggression" would be met with "much more severe and crushing measures." The Houthis, Iran's proxy in Yemen, seized the moment to declare their Red Sea ban.

## The EU's New Tool

The EU sanctions are significant not for their immediate economic impact — the specific individuals and entities targeted have not yet been publicly named — but for the precedent they set. This is the first time the EU has activated its freedom-of-navigation sanctions mechanism, a framework specifically designed to punish states that weaponise maritime chokepoints.

Kallas made clear that the tool would be applied again "where necessary." For India, which has carefully avoided taking sides in the broader conflict, the EU's move complicates an already delicate diplomatic position. New Delhi has called for dialogue and diplomacy. But the EU is now escalating with legal and economic instruments — and expects its trading partners to take note.

## What India Faces

The Indian foreign ministry on Monday expressed "utmost concern" over the renewed hostilities, calling on all parties to de-escalate. But concern is not a shipping lane. India's options are constrained by geography, by its dependence on energy imports, and by the fact that neither chokepoint is within its sphere of influence.

In the near term, Indian shipping companies and cargo operators face the prospect of routing around both corridors simultaneously — the Cape of Good Hope for Red Sea traffic, and overland or longer ocean routes for Gulf energy. Each alternative adds cost, time, and complexity.

For NRI families sending remittances home, the downstream effects are already visible. Higher shipping costs raise the price of imported goods. Costlier energy raises the price of everything else. The rupee, already under pressure from record foreign outflows and a ballooning oil import bill, faces another wave of depreciation risk.

India's ability to weather this dual chokepoint crisis depends on variables it does not control: whether the Iran ceasefire can be restored, whether the Houthis follow through on their Red Sea threat, and whether Western and Gulf partners can backfill the supply disruption fast enough.

For now, the world's two most important maritime bottlenecks are both in play. And India is downstream of both.
